title: Regular pay above the top of the position’s own published range
question: Where was a position’s regular pay more than a tenth above the top of the salary range the employer itself reported for it?
finding: 9,903 position-years at the City and the other San Francisco bodies had regular pay more than 10% and $10,000 above the reported range maximum. 7,123 of them sit in department-years where 40% or more of rows are above the range, which points to the range reported rather than the pay: San Francisco, Fire Department: 6,493 rows in 7 years (as much as 51.9% of the department); Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District, Bus Operators: 601 rows in 5 years (as much as 68.6% of the department); City College of San Francisco (Community College District), Ccsf-Custodial Services: 29 rows in 1 year (as much as 42.6% of the department). The other 2,780 (1,161 of them rows that also name a second position): San Francisco 2,340; Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District 251; City College of San Francisco (Community College District) 69; San Francisco Superior Court 59; BART 36; San Francisco Unified School District 24; Transbay Joint Powers Authority 1. At the City the largest groups are Public Health (1189), Police (260), Public Utilities Commission (201). Largest gap: Police Officer 3 (San Francisco, 2024), regular pay $634,859 against a top of $154,726.
how: State Controller raw export: regular pay against the export’s own “maximum position salary” for the row, where that maximum is $20,000 or more. The test needs both more than 10% and $10,000 above it. Department-years with 50 or more rows of which 40% or more fail the test are counted apart and not listed, because a whole department above its range is more likely a range reported on another basis (for example a shorter work week) than pay.
limits: Regular pay can include retroactive raises paid late, a mid-year promotion to a higher position, premiums folded into base pay, a 27th pay period or a leave cash-out; the reported range may be out of date or the wrong one. Each row is a question for the employer, not an overpayment.
